reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes pool shares as a way to earn Bitcoin, including a $500 share described as providing daily earnings for 1,000 days, and recommends the higher-priced Founder Pool. It directs prospective buyers to fund the purchase from an external Bitcoin wallet, send payment to a displayed address, and meet a 10-minute invoice deadline while urging them to take available offers. The claims and payment instructions are described, but mining activity, actual returns, and completed payment are not verified.

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker does not present every paid program as trustworthy. The description raises the concern of schemes running away with people's money, and the speaker tells viewers to choose according to what they can afford. Those are limited cautions, not proof that this particular service is safe, but they matter when assessing whether the presentation is simply an attempt to push viewers into the largest purchase. The recommendation for the Founder Pool is expressly conditional on affordability.

citations.quote: If you are tired of revshares shutting down or ponzi schemes and hiyp's running away with people's money
choose your shares according to your budget and what you can actually afford
if you can afford the founder pool then I recommend it

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies earnings claims and a payment route, but neither establishes that the speaker dismisses financial risk or insists on the highest-priced option. The affordability qualification narrows the Founder Pool recommendation. Likewise, a ten-minute invoice deadline is described as the invoice's expiration condition; the cited material does not establish that the speaker invented it to pressure viewers.

citations.quote: choose your shares according to your budget and what you can actually afford
you have 10 minutes to pay the invoice via Bitcoin before the invoice expires

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warning in the description refers to other schemes; it does not caution that these pool shares might fail to earn returns. The affordability qualifier accompanies a direct Founder Pool recommendation. More importantly, the speaker says a $500 share will earn Bitcoin every day and describes commissions paid to a wallet. Those claims, coupled with purchase guidance, remain the substance of the video.

citations.quote: If you are tired of revshares shutting down or ponzi schemes and hiyp's running away with people's money
if you can afford the founder pool then I recommend it
So this will be earning you bitcoin every day for a thousand days initially.

opening.argument: Judge, this is structured as an operational walkthrough: the title identifies a purchase tutorial, and the speaker says the purpose is to explain how the pools work and how to choose one. The explanation compares commission and repurchase percentages across pools, then walks through what happens after an invoice is generated. A demonstration of an interface can repeat its stated terms without independently proving them. The absence of verification should therefore limit confidence in the service's claims, not automatically turn an instructional video into evidence of deception.

citations.quote: How to Purchase a Mining Pool on Bitclub Network.
let's take a look at this and explain exactly how it works and how to choose your pool
pool two you get 60 percent commission paid your Bitcoin wallet and forty percent is used to repurchase and pool three is 70% commission and a 30% repurchase
an invoice will be generated and you have 10 minutes to pay the invoice via Bitcoin before the invoice expires

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats the walkthrough's purchase steps as solicitation, but explaining where an invoice appears and when it expires is also ordinary tutorial content. Its point that returns are unverified is fair; the transcript does not show completed mining or a completed payment. The question is whether describing an unverified process itself establishes deception, and the cited steps do not settle that.

citations.quote: when you click buy now for example on the 500 pool one, an invoice will be generated
When you make that payment you will then have the shares show up in your account once it's processed.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it a tutorial does not remove the promotional claim at its center. The speaker tells viewers they need to purchase a share to start earning Bitcoin, presents daily earnings from a $500 share as an expected result, and recommends the Founder Pool to those who can afford it. The walkthrough then gives the Bitcoin payment procedure. Those are purchase-directed earnings claims, not merely neutral instruction about an interface.

citations.quote: you need to purchase a share in one of the pools, the Mining pools
So this will be earning you bitcoin every day for a thousand days initially.
if you can afford the founder pool then I recommend it

opening.argument: Judge, the visible offer can be read as a priced service with different terms: the page lists four pool choices, and the speaker explains that mining equipment needs replacement as technology changes. The payment is presented as buying a share, not as a fee for access to secret earning instructions. The cited material does show an upfront Bitcoin purchase, so that concern should not be minimized. But it does not show a request for wallet credentials, a demonstrated downline payout, or a fixed amount of profit. The percentages describe how purported mining proceeds would be allocated, which is narrower than proof of a guaranteed profit.

citations.quote: needs to buy new machines or upgrade the equipment in order to keep the mining pools running as efficiently as possible
50% of your Commission's would be paid into your Bitcoin wallet and 50% will be used to repurchase
you need to click the Buy Now and BICCLUB only accepts Bitcoins

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening says mining activity and returns are unverified; that cuts both ways. It identifies a paid offer and optimistic earnings language, but supplies no independent finding about whether the service mines or pays. The purchase page establishes a payment mechanism, not by itself a false one. The speaker's account of reinvesting proceeds in equipment offers an alternative reading of the repurchase term, even though the video does not verify that account.

citations.quote: needs to buy new machines or upgrade the equipment in order to keep the mining pools running as efficiently as possible

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing credential request or fixed profit figure does not resolve the concern. The speaker explicitly links the upfront share purchase to daily Bitcoin earnings and says wallet commissions will be paid, while the page offers shares for purchase. The equipment explanation is the speaker's claim, not evidence that the machines or payouts exist. The relevant mechanism is paying for purported mining returns, which the video presents directly.
